en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 25.1 (SN 25.1, PTS SN iii 225) 1. The Chapter on the Eye (Cakkhuvagga) The Discourse on the Eye (Cakkhusutta)
At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration;
the ear is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.”
The nose is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise;
the tongue is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise;
the body is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
The mind is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.

Monks, one who has such faith and conviction in these things is called a follower by faith. He has entered the fixed course of rightness, entered the plane of true persons, and transcended the plane of worldlings.
He is incapable of performing that deed by which, having performed it, he would be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
And he is incapable of passing away until he has realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Monks, one for whom these teachings are thus sufficiently approved by wisdom through reflection is called a "follower of Dhamma. He has entered the certainty of rightness, entered the plane of true persons, and transcended the plane of worldlings.
He is incapable of performing such an action that, having performed it, he would be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
"And he is incapable of passing away until he has realized the fruit of stream-entry.

"Bhikkhus, one who understands these things thus and sees them thus is called a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. Thus was the first [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 25.2 (SN 25.2, PTS SN iii 225) 1. Cakkhuvagga Rūpasutta (The Discourse on Form) “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self; what is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Feeling is impermanent... Perception is impermanent... Volitional formations are impermanent... Consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self; what is non-self should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion towards form, revulsion towards feeling, revulsion towards perception, revulsion towards volitional formations, revulsion towards consciousness. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, forms are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise;
sounds are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise.”
Odors are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration;
tastes are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration;
tangibles are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
"Phenomena are impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.

Monks, whoever has such faith and conviction in these phenomena is called a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*). He has entered the fixed course of rightness, entered the plane of true persons, and transcended the plane of worldlings.
He is incapable of performing that deed by which, having performed it, he would be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts."
And he is incapable of passing away until he has realized the fruit of stream-entry.

Monks, one for whom these phenomena are thus sufficiently approved by wisdom through reflection is called a "follower of Dhamma. He has entered upon the certainty of rightness, entered the plane of the true person, and transcended the plane of the worldling.
He is incapable of performing such an action that, having performed it, he would be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
"And he is incapable of passing away until he realizes the fruit of stream-entry.
"Monks, whoever understands these things thus and sees them thus, is called a stream-enterer,
no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his final goal."
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 25.3 (SN 25.3, PTS SN iii 226) 1.
The Chapter on the Eye (Cakkhuvagga)
The Discourse on Consciousness. Setting: Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, eye-consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration;”
Ear-consciousness … nose-consciousness … tongue-consciousness …
Body-consciousness … mind-consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise.
Whoever, monks, … [as before] … [is practicing for the complete destruction of suffering].
“...having full enlightenment as its ultimate goal.
Thus [he spoke]. The third [discourse]. *Saṁyutta Nikāya* 25.4 (SN 25.4, PTS SN iii 226).
1. Cakkhuvagga Samphassasutta.
Setting at Savatthi.
“Eye-contact, bhikkhus, is impermanent, subject to change, and bound to become otherwise;
ear-contact … nose-contact …”
Tongue-contact … body-contact … mind-contact is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration.
“Monks, whoever has such faith and resolve regarding these teachings is called a ‘follower by faith’ … [as before] … one whose ultimate destination is full enlightenment.
This is the fourth [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 25.5 (SN 25.5, PTS SN iii 226) 1. Cakkhuvagga Samphassajasutta (The Discourse on Born of Contact) “Bhikkhus, born of eye-contact, there arises what is felt; born of ear-contact... born of nose-contact... born of tongue-contact... born of body-contact... born of mind-contact, there arises what is felt. If one does not understand as they really are the origin and the passing away of that which is born of mind-contact, one is not a stream-enterer, one who is no longer subject to perdition, assured, bound for enlightenment. But if one understands as they really are the origin and the passing away of that which is born of mind-contact, one is a stream-enterer, one who is no longer subject to perdition, assured, bound for enlightenment.”
At Sāvatthī.
"Monks, feeling born of eye-contact is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration;
feeling born of ear-contact is [the same]... [and so on]."
Feeling born of nose-contact … feeling born of tongue-contact … feeling born of body-contact … [and so on] …
“Feeling born of mind-contact is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
Monks, whoever has such faith and conviction in these things is called a ‘follower by faith’ … [and so on] … one whose ultimate destination is full enlightenment.”
The Fifth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 25.6 (SN 25.6, PTS SN iii 227) 1.
Cakkhuvagga (The Chapter on the Eye)
The Discourse on Perceptions of Form.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, perceptions of form are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration."
perception of sound … perception of odor … perception of taste …
Perception of tangibles … perception of mental phenomena is impermanent, subject to change,
and subject to alteration. Monks, one who has such faith and conviction in these things is called a “follower by faith” … [and so on].
“...having full enlightenment as its ultimate goal. The sixth [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 25.7 (SN 25.7, PTS SN iii 227).
1. Cakkhuvagga:
Rūpasañcetanāsutta.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Volitional formations regarding forms, bhikkhus, are impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise;
volitional formations regarding sounds … volitional formations regarding odors …”
Volition regarding tastes … volition regarding tangibles … volition regarding mental phenomena is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise.
“Monks, whoever has such faith and resolve in these teachings is called a ‘follower by faith’ … [as before] … one whose ultimate destination is full enlightenment. Thus was the seventh [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 25.8 (SN 25.8, PTS SN iii 227) 1. Cakkhuvagga Rūpataṇhāsutta (Craving for Forms) “Bhikkhus, craving for forms arises dependent on form; it does not arise apart from form. Craving for sounds... craving for odors... craving for tastes... craving for tactile objects... craving for mental phenomena arises dependent on mental phenomena; it does not arise apart from mental phenomena.”
At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, craving for forms is impermanent, subject to change, and liable to become otherwise;
craving for sounds …”
craving for odors … craving for tastes … craving for tangibles …
“Craving for phenomena is impermanent, subject to change,
and subject to alteration. Whoever, monks, has such faith and resolve regarding these phenomena is called a ‘follower by faith’ … [as before] … one whose destiny is full enlightenment.”
Eighth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 25.9 (SN 25.9, PTS SN iii 227) 1.
Cakkhuvagga (The Chapter on the Eye)
The Discourse on the Earth Element. At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, the earth element is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration."
the water element … the fire element … the air element …
The space element ...
the consciousness element is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise.
Monks, one who has such faith and resolve in these phenomena is called a "follower by faith" ... [and so on].
“...having full enlightenment as his final goal. Thus [ends] the ninth.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 25.10 (SN 25.10, PTS SN iii 227).
1. The Chapter on the Eye.
Discourse on the Aggregates.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, form is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration;
feeling is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to alteration;
perception is….”
Volitional formations are impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise;
consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, and subject to becoming otherwise.

Monks, one who has such faith and resolve regarding these phenomena is called a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*); he has entered the certainty of rightness, has entered the plane of the true person, and has transcended the plane of the worldling.
He is incapable of performing such an action that, having performed it, he would be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts;
and he is incapable of passing away until he realizes the fruit of stream-entry.

Monks, one for whom these qualities are thus sufficiently approved by wisdom after reflection is called a "follower of Dhamma. He has entered the fixed course of rightness, he has entered the plane of true persons, and he has transcended the plane of ordinary worldlings.
He is incapable of performing such an action that, having performed it, he would be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts;
and he is incapable of passing away until he has realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Monks, one who understands these things thus and sees them thus is called:
‘A stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his final goal. Tenth.
The First Chapter on the Eye.
Its summary verse:
Eye, form, and consciousness,
contact, and feeling.
Perception, volition, and craving—
these ten, by way of the aggregates, are the elements.
The Connected Discourse on Descent is finished.
